findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Forecast in-year overspend of £335k for 2026/27 despite corporate contingency use, driven by Children's, Adult Social Care, and Environment
findings.detail: The Q1 position shows a forecast overspend of £335k for the full year 2026/27. The main overspend areas are: Children's Services (cost of children in care and home-to-school transport); Adult Social Care (hospital discharge, increased eligible population, increased acuity); Environment (planning and bereavement income shortfalls). These are being partially offset by contingent resources set aside in the budget, but the register notes the forecast overspend is "now exceeding the council's in-year corporate contingency and the limited time in which to deliver additional mitigation."
findings.matters: A lender sees that despite contingency use and mitigation attempts, the council is still forecast to overspend in-year on demographic and demand pressures that show no sign of easing.
findings.figures: £335k forecast overspend; corporate contingency is circa £4m per annum
findings.quote: The council is projecting a materially balanced position (£335k forecast overspend) for 2026/27. The main forecast areas of overspending are Children's Services: including both the cost of supporting those children in the care of the authority, and home to school transport. Adult Social Care: High levels of hospital discharge, increases in the number of people eligible for support, and increases in the acuity of need.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Waste contract risk improved from VERY HIGH to HIGH; interim two-year contract in place pending longer-term procurement
findings.detail: Risk 18 shows improvement from 25 VERY HIGH (December 2025) to 15 HIGH (current). The council has negotiated and mobilised a two-year interim contract with Veolia commencing 1 April 2026, providing continuity of statutory waste services after exit from the previous PPP contract. The council received a settlement sum from the previous contract. However, the register notes expected cost pressures from recyclate rebasing and the council must procure a longer-term solution by 1 April 2028.
findings.matters: A risk that threatened service failure has been mitigated with a stable interim contract, but the council must re-procure within two years and faces cost volatility from recycling markets.
findings.figures: Contract term: 1 April 2026 to 1 April 2028; score improved from 25 to 15
findings.quote: Risk score reduced this period due to the interim contract with Veolia but remains high as waste team procure a longer-term solution to 1 April 2028.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Highways PFI contract risk substantially reduced from VERY HIGH to MEDIUM after resolving pricing disputes
findings.detail: Risk 20 shows significant improvement. The current score is 10 MEDIUM (down from 25 VERY HIGH in December 2025). The register notes: "differences in interpretation regarding pricing were resolved in July 2025 and both design and construction work is being commissioned and implemented." The reset action plan has worked and is now business as usual. NISTA funding for transformational change extended to March 2027. Two of three major workstreams complete.
findings.matters: A material operational and financial risk that has been a concern (assessed VERY HIGH only nine months ago) has been substantially mitigated. This is material good news for a lender: a council managing a very large PFI contract successfully through a dispute and reset is a positive signal of management capability during stress.
findings.figures: Score reduced from 25 (Dec 25) to 10 (Sep 26); 2/3 workstreams complete; NISTA funding to March 2027
findings.quote: Current score reduced to 10 MEDIUM, the differences in interpretation regarding pricing were resolved in July 2025 and both design and construction work is being commissioned and implemented.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer post vacant with significant recruitment challenges, creating instability in key statutory finance role
findings.detail: Risk 3 (Organisational Capacity) notes "There have been significant challenges in recruitment to the Director of Finance and s151 Officer post, leaving instability in a key senior role." The Section 151 Officer is the council's statutory financial officer and chief architect of its budget and financial strategy. An vacant post at this level is material instability at a time when the council is managing EFS and structural deficits of unprecedented scale.
findings.matters: A lender depends on stable financial leadership and the statutory officer's personal accountability for financial legality and proper accounting. A prolonged vacancy creates risk of continuity gaps, slower decision-making, and loss of institutional memory at a critical moment.
findings.figures: One director-level role unfilled; no timeline given for recruitment
findings.quote: There have been significant challenges in recruitment to the Director of Finance and s151 Officer post, leaving instability in a key senior role

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support triggers External Assurance Review by Grant Thornton, with subsequent councils often receiving Best Value Notice
findings.detail: The council's receipt of EFS 'in principle' means it will be subject to an External Assurance Review undertaken by Grant Thornton on behalf of government. The risk register notes that "a number of authorities who have had EARs undertaken subsequently receive a Best Value Notice." A Best Value Notice is a formal government intervention measure. The risk register also notes that governance improvement activity remains at early stage and external auditor scrutiny is a significant factor in assessing effectiveness.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council is now subject to formal government oversight and faces material risk of a Best Value Notice, which is a statutory intervention that restricts council powers.
findings.figures: Grant Thornton undertaking EAR; governance improvement still early stage
findings.quote: Due to receiving "in principle" Exceptional Financial Support the council will be subject to an External Assurance Review (EAR) which will be undertaken by Grant Thornton on behalf of government - a number of authorities who have had EARs undertaken subsequently receive a Best Value Notice.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Structural deficits forecast to grow to £40m in 2027/28 and £66m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The February 2026 Full Council instructed Directors to plan for a structural deficit of £40m for 2027/28, rising to £66m by 2029/30. An Improvement Board has been established to address this, with transformation plans to be incorporated into service business plans. These are projected figures, not current year actuals, but they represent the medium-term trajectory the council's leadership expects absent major service reductions or funding changes.
findings.matters: A lender seeing structural deficits of this scale three years out needs to understand whether the council has a funded or credible transformation plan to close them, and what service cuts or income changes this will require.
findings.quote: February Council instructed Directors to start planning how the Council will identify savings opportunities to contribute towards a Transformation Plan to address the forecast "Structural" Deficit of £40m for 2027/28, rising to £66m by 2029/30

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Council needed £12.9m government emergency loan to set a legal 2026/27 budget despite actual structural deficit of £20.4m
findings.detail: The council applied for and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) permission to borrow £12.9m to achieve a legally balanced position. The document states explicitly that without one-off resources, the underlying structural deficit is £20.4m. This is a deficit closed not by operational action but by emergency government lending, the only mechanism available to councils unable to balance a budget conventionally.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council cannot balance its budget without government emergency support, and that the underlying gap is 58% larger than the money borrowed to cover it.
findings.figures: £12.9m loan; £20.4m underlying structural deficit in 2026/27
findings.quote: Setting a legally balanced budget position for 2026/27 was only possible because the council applied for and received permission to drawdown a £12.9m loan. The underlying structural deficit in 2026/27 is £20.4m (it is only via the use of one-off resources that the amount has been reduced to £12.9m).

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: External audit opinions for 2024/25 and prior years were disclaimed due to limited audit timeframe in reset phase; full audit planned for 2025/26 accounts autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The council met the February 2026 backstop date for 2024/25 audit completion following national audit delays. However, auditors issued disclaimed opinions due to insufficient time to gather reliable evidence during the audit reset phase. A full audit is planned for autumn 2026 for the 2025/26 accounts to meet the January 2027 backstop date.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions remove external validation of financial statement reliability; lenders cannot rely on auditor assurance until full audits resume; auditor confidence deficit extends lender uncertainty about account quality.
findings.figures: February 2026 backstop date for 2024/25 audits met; disclaimed opinions issued; January 2027 backstop date for 2025/26; full audit planned autumn 2026
findings.quote: Like a significant proportion of local authorities, the limited timeframe for reset has meant auditors have not had sufficient time to gain enough reliable, appropriate evidence and have therefore issued disclaimed opinions on the accounts for recent years.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Pension Fund compliance with new Pension Act deadline of 30 June 2026 appears unlikely; fund may need to self-report to Pension Regulator.
findings.detail: A new Pension Act effective 30 June 2026 requires local government pension funds to join FCA-regulated investment pools. Although work continues for the Isle of Wight Pension Fund to join the Central investment pool, 'it looks increasing unlikely this will be feasible by 30 June 2026, meaning a self-report to the Pension Regulator will need to be considered.' Internal Audit identified three high-risk findings: action plan unrealistic expectations, inconsistent knowledge/understanding completion, and contributions reconciliation gaps.
findings.matters: Pension fund compliance failure and Pension Regulator self-report flag governance weakness affecting scheme members and attracting regulatory scrutiny; indicates capacity constraints preventing timely regulatory deadline compliance.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 regulatory deadline; three high-risk audit findings on action plan pace, knowledge & understanding, and contributions reconciliation
findings.quote: At the time of writing, although work is continuing for the IWC pension Fund to join the Central investment pool, it looks increasing unlikely this will be feasible by 30 June 2026, meaning a self-report to the Pension Regulator will need to be considered.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Adult Social Care CQC assessment rated the service as 'requires improvement', though a separate Ofsted review of care leavers arrangements was positive.
findings.detail: The council received a CQC assessment of Adult Services rated as 'requires improvement'. This is noted in the context of broader organizational stress and increased whistle-blowing investigations. A separate Ofsted review of care leavers arrangements was positive, providing mixed signal on service quality.
findings.matters: Regulator concern about a major spending area (costs up £14.8m, 21% increase) signals service delivery and quality issues; regulators may impose intervention affecting operations or reputation; cost escalation and quality concerns compound financial risk.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care costs up £14.8m (21%); CQC rating 'requires improvement'; Ofsted care leavers review positive
findings.quote: the recent CQC assessment of Adult Services rated the service as 'requires improvement', although the Ofsted review of arrangements for care leavers earlier this year was positive.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Governance culture and constitutional compliance issues identified by statutory officers, including lack of respect for constitutional framework, potential Member-Officer Protocol breaches, and adversarial behaviours requiring external facilitated engagement.
findings.detail: Statutory officers raised concerns about organizational culture and governance. Key issues include lack of respect for the constitutional framework, potential breaches of the Member-Officer Protocol and Members Code of Conduct, adversarial behaviours, disregard for professional advice, and challenges to decision-making processes. The council has engaged senior councillors, developed a member development strategy and delivered an externally facilitated engagement programme to address these issues.
findings.matters: Governance culture failures compromise decision-making quality, undermine officer advice, create reputational risk, and indicate organizational dysfunction; they signal deeper control environment weakness beyond formal processes.
findings.figures: External facilitation required; new Standards Committee established but not yet meeting; comprehensive induction programme delivered
findings.quote: Key issues related to a lack of respect for the constitutional framework, including potential breaches of the Member-Officer Protocol, Members Code of Conduct, adversarial behaviours, lack of respect for professional advice and regular challenges to decision-making processes.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer and Director of Finance posts are being recruited following wind-down of strategic partnership with Portsmouth City Council; currently operating under interim arrangements.
findings.detail: The council previously obtained its Director of Finance, Section 151 Officer and Chief Internal Auditor roles through a strategic partnership with Portsmouth City Council. This arrangement is ending, and the council is recruiting its own finance leadership for 2026/27. Recruitment is underway but currently supported through interim arrangements.
findings.matters: Continuity and quality of senior finance leadership is critical to financial resilience; interim arrangements during a financial crisis period increase delivery risk; permanent recruitment may delay while council faces structural deficit.
findings.figures: S151 Officer and Director of Finance recruitment underway; interim arrangement in place; recruitment timeline to 2026/27
findings.quote: Recruitment is underway for the appointment of a dedicated S151 Officer and Director of Finance and for the Assistant Director of Finance. This is currently supported through an interim arrangement.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Waste contract contractor became financially unstable and the contract was terminated on 31 March 2026, requiring emergency management and new two-year interim procurement.
findings.detail: The waste contract risk reached a critical point due to the contractor's financial instability, forcing termination on 31 March 2026. The council managed the exit and secured waste service delivery for two years while undertaking a comprehensive procurement exercise for long-term arrangements, leaving the permanent solution uncertain.
findings.matters: Critical service delivery risk materialized and required emergency intervention; demonstrates vulnerability of large outsourced contracts and council's ability to manage contractor failure during a period of financial stress.
findings.figures: Waste contract termination 31 March 2026; two-year interim arrangement; service delivery secured pending procurement outcome
findings.quote: The waste contract risk reached a critical point due to the financial instability of the Council's waste contractor and the impending termination of that contract on 31 March 2026. This exit was effectively managed, and the delivery of waste services secured for the next two years.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Resource shortfalls have worsened materially in 2025/26 and are expected to continue through 2026/27, compromising the control environment during forced organizational change.
findings.detail: Internal Audit identified limited resources as a root cause of governance issues in 2024/25, and this has deteriorated. The statement notes 'both the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact having worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.' As a condition of exceptional funding, the council must prepare a transformation plan requiring significant change, placing further strain on already reduced capacity.
findings.matters: Resource constraints during mandatory recovery reduce capacity to execute change and maintain controls, increasing likelihood of service failures and control breakdowns; worsening capacity during financial crisis indicates loss of organizational resilience.
findings.figures: Resource shortfall identified, impact worsening from 2024/25 through 2025/26, trend expected to continue through 2026/27
findings.quote: In 2024/25 Internal Audit identified limited resources as a root cause of many issues. This continues to be the case but with both the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact having worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Internal Audit issued a 'no assurance' report for the first time in 2025/26, with high-risk findings increasing and audit opinion at risk of downgrade in 2026/27.
findings.detail: 2025/26 saw the first 'no assurance' audit report and two 'limited assurance' ratings, departing from prior years' mostly 'assurance' or 'reasonable assurance' ratings. High-risk findings increased within 'reasonable assurance' audits. The overall annual opinion remains 'reasonable assurance', but Internal Audit notes 'the direction of travel indicates that there is a risk that that the audit opinion for 2026/2027 may not sustain this position.'
findings.matters: Deteriorating audit opinions signal weakening control environment and governance effectiveness; a downgrade from reasonable to limited or no assurance would indicate material governance failure affecting financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: One 'no assurance' report; two 'limited assurance' ratings; increased high-risk findings within reasonable assurance audits in single year
findings.quote: 2025/26 has seen a 'no assurance' report issued by Internal Audit, with a further two areas rated 'limited assurance'. Across audits rated 'reasonable assurance' the number of individual findings rated 'high risk' has also increased.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Council required exceptional financial support from government to set 2026/27 budget, with a structural deficit of £20m rising to £65m by 2029/30 if unaddressed.
findings.detail: The council was one of 37 authorities requiring Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27, with government permission to borrow £12.9m for day-to-day operational expenditure. The underlying structural deficit stems from £14.8m escalation in Adult Social Care costs, £6.5m doubling of waste contract costs, and £13.8m reduction in government funding over three years. Without intervention, the deficit could reach £65m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: Government intervention to balance a budget indicates financial unsustainability and puts the council in dependency on exceptional support while developing a recovery plan; this signals fundamental affordability issues for lenders.
findings.figures: £12.9m borrowing approval for operational expenditure; £20m structural deficit 2026/27; potential £65m by 2029/30; Adult Social Care £14.8m (21% increase); waste contract £6.5m doubling; government funding reduction £13.8m over 3 years (16%)
findings.quote: The setting of the Isle of Wight Councils budget for 2026/27 was its most challenging for at least the last ten-year period. A legally balanced budget was only achievable through the direct support of government and through their Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) programme

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Four major reserves—General Fund, Capital Grants Unapplied, Revaluation Reserve, and Capital Adjustment Account—carry unaudited brought-forward balances from 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.detail: These reserves carry opening balances from the disclaimed audit years that were never independently verified. Post-disclaimer audit procedures focused only on current-year movements, not underlying balances. The General Fund and Capital Adjustment Account are both described as material and highly complex.
findings.matters: Unaudited reserve balances mean the council's stated financial position and available resources lack independent verification for 2-3 years of cumulative transactions, materially undermining statement reliability.
findings.figures: Four reserves affected; balances at 31 March 2023 and 2024 unaudited
findings.quote: Whilst audit procedures in subsequent years have provided assurance over movements in the General Fund, the closing balances at 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024 were not audited due to the disclaimer of opinion. Consequently, assurance has not been obtained over the underlying brought-forward balances.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Audit fees will vary beyond the standard scale fee due to additional work on reserve rebuild and historical assurance procedures.
findings.detail: EY explicitly states that activities relating to the reserve risk assessment and rebuilding of historical assurance are outside the scale fee. The auditor is seeking a formal variation to the scale fee, indicating material additional costs beyond the baseline audit contract.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs reflect the council's need for more intensive work due to control and documentation gaps, adding financial pressure.
findings.figures: Variation amount TBD; services outside April 2026 planning scope
findings.quote: procedures relating to the rebuilding of historical assurance will also be outside the scale fee. Accordingly, we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Two unresolved accounting issues identified in 2024/25—waste asset valuation and school IFRS 16 treatment—remain to be addressed in 2025/26.
findings.detail: EY identified a waste asset valuation matter affecting the revaluation reserve and a schools IFRS 16 consideration affecting the capital adjustment account. Both issues are expected to be resolved in 2025/26. These represent known accounting uncertainties that originated in the disclaimed years and have carried forward.
findings.matters: Known unresolved accounting issues indicate control and documentation weaknesses that affect financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Two matters identified 2024/25; resolution expected 2025/26
findings.quote: In 24/25, a specific outstanding matter relating to waste asset valuation was identified, which may impact the revaluation reserve. In 2024–25, a specific matter relating to the consideration of schools under IFRS 16 has been identified, which may impact the Capital Adjustment Account.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: The council's path to an unqualified audit opinion extends to at least 2029/30 or beyond, constrained by a 5-year property revaluation cycle.
findings.detail: EY notes that properties last valued in the disclaimed years 2022/23 and 2023/24 will not be revalued until 2027/28 and 2028/29. The auditor states it cannot move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion until this revaluation cycle is completed, meaning unqualified status is not achievable until after that work is done.
findings.matters: Extended periods of qualified or disclaimed opinions restrict the council's access to capital markets and increase borrowing costs, as lenders price in elevated risk.
findings.figures: 5-year valuation cycle; next revaluation due 2027/28-2028/29
findings.quote: The Council has a 5 year rolling programme and properties last valued in 2022/23 and 2023/24, both disclaimed, would next be valued in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Therefore, we may not be able to move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion until this cycle is completed.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Isle of Wight received disclaimer opinions in 2023/24 and 2024/25 on reserves, property/plant/equipment, cash flow and other core financial statement areas.
findings.detail: The council's auditors issued disclaimers due to the statutory backstop and inability to complete planned audit procedures across multiple key areas. This represents the second consecutive year the council could not obtain a clean audit opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means the auditor could not form a conclusion on whether the financial statements are fairly stated—a material concern for any lender assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 2023/24 and 2024/25 audits; disclaimer across Property, plant and equipment, Reserves, Comprehensive Income and Expenditure, Cash Flow, Collection Fund, Other disclosures
findings.quote: In 20 23/24 and 2024/25, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop and planned audit procedures not being completed in the following areas: Property, plant and equipment, Reserves, Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, Cash Flow Statement, Collection Fund, Other disclosures

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 4 - Responses to Audit and Governance Committee questions from July 2026 committee (1)
findings.headline: Council acknowledges it cannot systematically publish required contract details notices due to resource constraints.
findings.detail: When asked to include contract details notices in reporting, the council disclosed that no action has yet been taken on this requirement. It explained that determining which contracts require notices requires case-by-case review, and that there is currently 'no streamlined means of manually updating this within the reports with current resources.' The council stated this will be reviewed in future.
findings.matters: A council that acknowledges being unable to meet contract transparency requirements due to resource constraints signals both a control gap and resourcing issue that lenders assess when evaluating governance quality and management capacity.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: No action has yet been carried out in regard to this ask.  The requirement as to whether to publish a Contract Details Notices or not are varied and need review on a case by case basis.  Currently there is no streamlined means of manually updating this within the reports with current resources.  This will be a point for review at some point in the future.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Procurement Half-Yearly Report
findings.headline: Procurement team is understaffed with ongoing resource gaps affecting its ability to deliver oversight in timely manner.
findings.detail: The team is described as 'relatively small' with 'ongoing resourcing gaps' despite responsibility for contracts over £30,000 (inc. VAT) across all directorates. The report notes that 'capacity demands impact ability to deliver all procurement related projects in timely manner.'
findings.matters: Procurement oversight is a key financial control; an understaffed team risks failures in compliance monitoring, spending scrutiny, and contract management.
findings.figures: No staff numbers disclosed; team responsible for contracts over £30,000 inc. VAT
findings.quote: The team is relatively small in size and has responsibility for delivering a wide range of statutory, governance and operational procurement functions, which is further compounded by ongoing resourcing gaps within the team.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Procurement Half-Yearly Report
findings.headline: Council has identified significant gaps in its procurement data collection that prevent reliable comparison to historical records.
findings.detail: Officers reviewed how procurement data was captured and found inconsistencies and gaps requiring remediation. The contract register shows £1.20bn in contracts, but some entries lack stated values; the council states 'the actual figures are likely to be higher than shown above.' Direct comparison to prior years cannot be assured due to these historical gaps.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can accurately track and report on financial commitments; data quality gaps in procurement suggest control weaknesses that could mask other financial risks.
findings.figures: 383 contracts on register (whole life value £1.20 billion); some lack stated contract values
findings.quote: As a consequence of these changes, together with inconsistencies and gaps identified in the previous processes, direct comparison with historic data cannot be fully assured.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Strategic Risk Register v2
findings.headline: CMT has identified a new strategic risk that significant government policy changes will outpace the council's organisational readiness, risking statutory non-compliance, unfunded mandates and financial pressures.
findings.detail: The council's Corporate Management Team has added a new strategic risk to the register relating to government policy changes including the Families First Programme, Social Work Reform, NHS 10-Year Plan, Local Government Reorganisation, Devolution settlements, and Planning & Infrastructure Act. The risk is that policy changes will introduce statutory duties, funding conditions, structural changes, and reporting requirements faster than the council can implement them. Consequences explicitly identified by the council include financial pressures (overspends, cost of compliance, stranded costs during reorganisation), disruption to critical children's, adults, health and care services, legal challenges, workforce turnover, partnership breakdown, and capital programme delays.
findings.matters: A lender would care because unfunded mandates, statutory non-compliance, and financial pressures from unplanned policy changes could significantly impact the council's financial position, service delivery capability, and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: CMT have identified the risk that significant changes from new or amended government policy will outpace organisational readiness, leading to statutory non‑compliance, unfunded mandates, disruption to critical services (children's, adults, health & care, planning, and infrastructure), workforce shortages, partnership fragmentation, and reputational harm.

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026
findings.headline: Control weaknesses in billing and charging processes for adult social care services
findings.detail: Two audits identified control issues in adult social care billing. WightCare audit found one overbilling case in a sample of 30 invoices, with lack of documentation and limited checking. ASC Charges audit identified inconsistent guidance on charging assessments, billing discrepancies including delayed processing and over/under payments, and unclear public communication of complaint procedures.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in income collection systems create risk of lost revenue, underrecovery of costs, customer disputes, and cash flow uncertainty—material for a lender assessing the council's ability to sustain adult social care operations.
findings.figures: 1 overbilling instance in sample of 30 invoices
findings.quote: A number of issues were identified regarding billing, invoicing and chargeable services, including lack of documentation, one instance of overbilling (out of a sample of 30) and limited checking in the billing process

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026
findings.headline: Multiple system access control and security patching weaknesses in network infrastructure
findings.detail: The Local Network audit identified several control weaknesses: 36 staff hold administrative system access (higher than normally expected, though work is underway to restrict this); 10 of 38 Linux servers run unsupported versions; 4 of 156 Windows servers have unconfirmed patching status. Additionally, 27% of staff access provisioning and 32% of access removal requests were made after effective dates.
findings.matters: Weak access controls and outdated or unpatched systems create cybersecurity and operational resilience risks that could compromise the council's ability to deliver services and protect sensitive data—material concerns for any lender evaluating operational stability.
findings.figures: 36 with admin access (higher than normal), 10 of 38 Linux servers out-of-support, 4 of 156 Windows servers with unconfirmed patching, 27% starter provisioning delays, 32% leaver removal delays
findings.quote: The number of staff with administrative access is higher than normally observed (36), although this is partially due to duplication of accounts, associated with ongoing work to restrict access. While primarily based on MS Windows a small number of servers (38) are running versions of Linux. Of these a subset of ten are running out of support versions which, where possible, need to be updated.

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026
findings.headline: High-risk deficiency in expenditure controls and procurement procedures at Carisbrooke Primary School
findings.detail: Internal audit found that the school raises purchase orders only after receiving invoices, rather than in advance, and does not properly document order requests. Testing of five items of expenditure over £10,000 found that three lacked evidence that quotes had been sought, representing failure to follow basic procurement controls.
findings.matters: Failure to follow procurement procedures creates risk of overpaying, eliminates competitive tension in purchasing, and prevents effective budget management—a fundamental financial control concern for any lender or finance director.
findings.figures: 3 out of 5 items over £10,000 lacked quote evidence
findings.quote: The high risk finding relates to expenditure, due to order requests not being appended to purchase orders and purchase order only being raised once invoices are received rather than in advance. Audit testing also identified a lack of evidence to support quotes being sought for three items of expenditure (out of a sample of five) in excess of £10,000.

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026
findings.headline: High-risk deficiency in safeguarding arrangements in Mosaic children's services system
findings.detail: The audit of Mosaic (the council's case management system for children's services, implemented in 2025) identified a high-risk finding that key contract deliverables specified in the 2020 contract have not been met, particularly safeguarding arrangements and business continuity. The divergence arose because the actual implementation differs from the contract due to the council's exit from its Hampshire partnership and other changes over the five years between contract signature and implementation.
findings.matters: Safeguarding is a critical compliance and reputational issue for any council. Contractual non-compliance in a major children's services system represents a significant child protection and governance risk that would concern any lender assessing the authority's ability to manage critical services safely.
findings.figures: contract signed 2020, implementation 2025
findings.quote: a high-risk finding is raised regarding the key 'deliverables' identified in the 2020 Contract. These cover important areas, including business continuity and most significantly safeguarding arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 7e. Appendix 1 - Isle of Wight Council Treasury Management 25-26 Q4 02 FINAL
findings.headline: Council established £5m credit facility with Sovereign Network Homes; facility not drawn as of March 2026
findings.detail: Council committed £5m credit facility to housing association for 3 years (plus 2-year extension option). Council receives standing fee regardless of use; interest at 2.5% above base rate if drawn. Reflects council's involvement in local housing finance.

findings.detail: No breaches of the prudential indicators set for the 2026-27 year.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Treasury Management Report Quarter 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Borrowing costs achieved lower than budget through short-term borrowing strategy
findings.detail: With interest rates not rising from prior years, the council's short-term borrowing strategy has delivered lower than budgeted borrowing costs. Existing long-term borrowing is unaffected by rate movements.
findings.matters: Shows favorable treasury execution this quarter, but also reveals the council's dependence on stable or falling rates; refinancing risk becomes material if rates rise
findings.figures: No specific figures given; outcome described as lower than budget

findings.detail: Combination of reduced borrowing costs (from short-term borrowing strategy) and increased investment income (rates rose from 3.80% to 3.87%) produced a forecast saving of over £655K. This is being used to help mitigate wider council in-year budget pressures.

findings.figures: £655K forecast saving, investment rates 3.80% rising to 3.87%
findings.quote: The combination of reduced borrowing costs and increased investment income has resulted in a net forecast saving of over £655K contributing to mitigating wider council in-year budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Appendix 1 - Isle of Wight Council Treasury Management 26-27 Q1 FINAL
findings.headline: Forecast borrowing substantially below capital financing requirement, indicating sustainable long-term debt position
findings.detail: The liability benchmark—which estimates cumulative borrowing needed to fund capital and revenue plans while maintaining minimum £10 million cash reserves—shows forecast borrowing levels substantially below the Loans Capital Financing Requirement throughout the planning period. The council is expected to be a long-term borrower with manageable debt levels relative to infrastructure needs.
findings.matters: Lenders use the liability benchmark to assess whether a council is prudently managing debt relative to capital requirements. Borrowing well below the benchmark indicates repayment capacity, headroom for future needs, and lower refinancing pressure.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £173.4 million (30 June 2026); liability benchmark forecast shown graphically tracking well below the CFR line through 2054
findings.quote: As can be seen from above the forecast borrowing levels are substantially below the Loans CFR.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Appendix 1 - Isle of Wight Council Treasury Management 26-27 Q1 FINAL
findings.headline: Council must exit £38.2 million of commercial property investments before borrowing further, constraining capital funding options
findings.detail: The council holds £38.2 million of commercial property investments purchased before the CIPFA Prudential Code changed in 2021. The Code now prohibits councils from borrowing to invest primarily for financial return. The council explicitly states it will review options for exiting these investments before undertaking further borrowing, creating a hard constraint on capital funding capacity.
findings.matters: This restriction limits the council's ability to borrow for capital projects unless or until these investments are divested, reducing financial flexibility precisely when councils are evaluating spending on infrastructure and services.
findings.figures: £38.2 million in directly owned property; £44.0 million total non-treasury investments generating £2.0 million annual income at 5.24% return
findings.quote: The council currently holds £38.2m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Appendix 1 - Isle of Wight Council Treasury Management 26-27 Q1 FINAL
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs increased from 4.63% to 5.00% as the council relies more on expensive short-term loans
findings.detail: The average rate on the council's short-term loans rose from 4.63% on £36 million (31 March 2026) to 5.00% on £41 million (30 June 2026). This increase reflects the elevated Bank Base Rate of 3.75% and high short-dated market rates. The council simultaneously increased the volume of short-term borrowing despite rising costs.
findings.matters: This directly increases the council's annual interest bill and expands refinancing risk: when these loans mature, they must be rolled over at whatever market rates prevail, exposing the council to further rate rises.
findings.figures: £41 million at 5.00% (30 June 2026) vs £36 million at 4.63% (31 March 2026); short-term borrowing from other local authorities available at 4.0% to 4.5% during the quarter
findings.quote: The council's short-term borrowing cost has remained high with currently high Base Rate and short-dated market rates. The average rate on the council's short-term loans at 30 June 2026 on £41 million was 5.00%, this compares with 4.63% on £36 million loans 3 months ago.

findings.headline: Pension arrangements identified as key governance risk requiring monitoring
findings.detail: The internal audit opinion identifies risks associated with the council's pension arrangements as one of two key governance risks. These risks are monitored and reported through the Isle of Wight Pension Fund Committee governance arrangements and supported by action plans.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities represent material obligations on council balance sheets; lenders assess whether councils are managing these liabilities and pension fund governance effectively
findings.figures: None provided in this paper
findings.quote: Risks associated with the Council's pension arrangements. These risks are monitored and reported through the governance arrangements of the Isle of Wight Pension Fund Committee.

findings.paper_title: 7e. Treasury Management Report Quarter 4 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit review of treasury management controls provided highest level of assurance
findings.detail: The treasury management function was reviewed by internal auditors based on 2023-24 transactions and received the highest level of assurance rating on the operation of controls.
findings.matters: Treasury controls manage significant sums of council money. Clean audit at the highest assurance level provides confidence in the quality of financial controls over these transactions.
findings.quote: The most recent review which was based on the 2023-24 transactions provided the highest level of assurance on the operation of these controls.

findings.paper_title: 7e. Treasury Management Report Quarter 4 2025-26
findings.headline: Council advances loans to other local authorities and explicitly excludes those with S114 notices
findings.detail: Beyond money market fund investments, the council is making loans to other local authorities. The council has implemented a credit monitoring policy specifically prohibiting lending to any authority that has issued an S114 notice (a statutory notice indicating inability to set a balanced budget).
findings.matters: Inter-council lending creates counterparty credit risk. The S114 exclusion demonstrates credit discipline, but lenders need visibility of exposure to other councils' credit positions.
findings.figures: one other local authority
findings.quote: In addition to investing in money market funds the council has loans advanced to one other local authority. Close attention is taken to the financial situation of other local authorities, and no loans have been made to any authority that has issued a S114 notice.

findings.paper_title: 7e. Treasury Management Report Quarter 4 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's investment holdings decreased by £5m during the twelve-month period
findings.detail: The level of investments held by the council has fallen by £5m. These holdings are stated to be maintained for timing differences in income and expenditure, suggesting the reduction may reflect temporary cash positioning.
findings.matters: Changes in investment holdings affect the council's liquidity position and available cash buffers for managing cash-flow timing.
findings.quote: The actual level of investments has decreased by £5m during the twelve-month period of this report, held for the purpose of timing differences in income and expenditure.

findings.paper_title: 7e. Treasury Management Report Quarter 4 2025-26
findings.headline: Average interest rates on investments have fallen 78 basis points from 4.58% to 3.80%
findings.detail: As interest rates have fallen, the council's average returns on its investment portfolio have declined by 78bp during the twelve-month period. This reflects declining investment income in the falling rate environment.
findings.matters: Falling investment income is a structural change affecting the council's cash position and budget flexibility, though offset by lower borrowing costs.
findings.figures: from an average of 4.58% to 3.80%
findings.quote: Over the period of this report the average interest rates on investments, have decreased from an average of 4.58% to 3.80%.

findings.detail: Lower borrowing costs from decreased short-term borrowing, combined with investment income, have generated a £925K forecast saving for the year. The council explicitly notes this is supporting management of its wider budget pressures.
findings.matters: Material treasury contribution to budget management. A £925K saving demonstrates effective extraction of value from treasury function at a time when budget is under pressure.
findings.figures: over £925K
findings.quote: The combination of reduced borrowing costs and increased investment income has resulted in a net forecast saving of over £925K contributing to mitigating wider council in-year budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Property portfolio management lacks appropriate software system, strategic documentation, and proper filing controls
findings.detail: The Property Value for Money audit (Corporate Services) received a 'limited assurance' rating due to high-risk issues: lack of an appropriate software system to manage the portfolio (also flagged in 2024/25), gaps in records, and files stored on personal drives rather than shared folders—most significantly for rent reviews. A replacement system is anticipated by mid-2026. The council also lacks strategic documentation covering its approach to property portfolio management.
findings.matters: Weak property management controls over a material corporate asset (particularly rent reviews) indicate inability to realize value from the council's property portfolio and risk of lease arrangements that do not protect the council's interests. This is a balance-sheet matter for lenders.
findings.figures: Replacement software system anticipated by mid-2026
findings.quote: High risk issues were identified regarding the current lack of an appropriate software system (also highlighted in the 2024/25 Internal Audit Annual Report) to manage the portfolio, with related high-risk issues identified regarding gaps in records and filing of records on personal drives, rather than shared folders, most significantly in relation to rent reviews.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Limited assurance on Personal Assistance: 26 of 189 active PAs have expired DBS checks, two confirmed in sample
findings.detail: The Personal Assistance audit (Adult Services) received a 'limited assurance' rating. Testing found 26 of 189 active Personal Assistants recorded in the system had expired DBS checks. Sample testing of 10 records confirmed expired DBS checks in two instances. The service implemented immediate corrective actions, but this finding flags inadequate vetting controls over individuals providing care to vulnerable adults.
findings.matters: Expired DBS checks on personal care assistants indicate breakdown in safeguarding control over vulnerable adults. For a lender, this signals weak compliance with duty of care and child/adult protection frameworks, with potential reputational and legal liability.
findings.figures: 26 of 189 active PAs flagged as expired; sample of 10 confirmed 2 with expired checks
findings.quote: Of the 189 active PAs recorded in the Council's software system 26 are flagged as having expired DBS checks, with sample testing of a sample of ten confirming expired DBS checks in two instances.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Resource constraints worsening and contributing to audit findings; likely to continue through 2026/27
findings.detail: The CIA reports that 'resource constraints continue to be a contributing factor to a number of issues identified' and that 'the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact have worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.' The s151 Officer and committee will be informed if this impacts the ability to meet statutory audit requirements. Specialist IT audit skills are particularly limited (only 2 qualified officers).
findings.matters: Resource constraints that are worsening and expected to persist signal that the council is unable to fund or retain the capacity needed to maintain control environment strength. Combined with financial deterioration, this creates a negative feedback loop for control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Only 2 officers qualified in specialist IT auditing; training underway for third, fourth being identified
findings.quote: Resource constraints continue to be a contributing factor to a number of issues identified. The shortfall in resources and the resulting impact have worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's financial position deteriorating with exceptional funding support granted for recovery
findings.detail: The annual opinion explicitly states that at the organisational level, 'the Council's financial position continues to deteriorate, with exceptional funding support having been granted, to support the Council's recovery.' This exceptional support sits alongside resource constraints that are themselves worsening and expected to persist through 2026/27.
findings.matters: Deteriorating financial position requiring exceptional government funding is the baseline indicator for lender risk. It directly affects both repayment capacity and the environment in which service delivery controls operate.
findings.figures: Exceptional funding support granted (amount not disclosed in this document)
findings.quote: At the organisational level the Council's financial position continues to deteriorate, with exceptional funding support having been granted, to support the Council's recovery.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Sharp fall in implementation of audit recommendations: 47% closed vs 55% prior year, breaking seven-year improvement trend
findings.detail: Of 42 medium and higher-risk audit exceptions followed up during 2025/26, only 47% were closed, with 53% still in progress or open. This represents the first deterioration after seven years of gradual improvement during the Portsmouth partnership, with high-risk findings still open (3 of 25) and medium-risk findings still open (2 of 14).
findings.matters: Inability to implement audit recommendations signals weakness in management capacity to remediate control weaknesses. This trend reversal after sustained improvement is a red flag for a lender or finance director assessing management's ability to manage recovery.
findings.figures: 47% closed (2025/26) vs 55% closed (2024/25); 3 high-risk, 2 medium-risk, 1 low-risk exceptions still open; 53% of exceptions in progress or open
findings.quote: With 47% closed, compared to 55% in 2024/25. This ends the trend of gradual improvements observed during the seven years of the partnership with Portsmouth City Council.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Control environment deteriorating despite maintaining 'reasonable assurance' opinion
findings.detail: The CIA notes deterioration in the control environment in 2025/26: one audit produced 'no assurance' (none in 2024/25), the first critical risk finding has appeared (0 in 2024/25), and the number of medium-risk findings rose from 31 to 38. The council is explicitly described as 'an organisation under increased stress' and the CQC assessment of Adult Services rated it as 'requires improvement'.
findings.matters: An audit opinion that masks deteriorating underlying control strength is of particular concern to lenders. The direction of travel—not just the current state—matters for financial stability assessment.
findings.figures: Critical risk: 0 (2024/25) to 1 (2025/26); Medium risk findings: 31 (2024/25) to 38 (2025/26); No assurance audits: 0 (2024/25) to 1 (2025/26)
findings.quote: Taken together these all indicate an organisation under increased stress, which has and will continue to have an impact on the effectiveness of the control environment.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Critical audit finding on £600k EHCP direct payments with no approval, setup or monitoring controls
findings.detail: The Education Health Care Plans (EHCPs) audit resulted in a 'no assurance' opinion, the only such rating this year. Testing found that approximately £600,000 spent on direct payments lacked approval, setup, monitoring and auditing, with the risk of error or fraud assessed as 'very high'. Additionally, 31% of EHCP decisions in the sample were not made within the required six-week deadline.
findings.matters: This represents a critical control weakness in a high-value spending area with unmitigated fraud risk. Lenders rely on robust controls over discretionary payments, and a council unable to approve or monitor £600k of commitments signals fundamental control environment weakness.
findings.figures: £600,000 spent on direct payments; 31% of sample decisions missed six-week deadline
findings.quote: In 2024/25 approximately £600,000 was spent on direct payments, with sample testing identifying a lack of approval, setup, monitoring and auditing the risk of error/fraud being assessed as very high.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: The council's audit recovery progress is one year behind the NAO's LARRIG 01 schedule, stemming from failure to produce accounts on time in 2023/24.
findings.detail: The council was expected to recover to qualified opinion by 2025/26, but is now only one year into recovery from 2024/25 baseline. This delay was caused by limited procedures in 2022/23 and again in 2023/24 when the council 'failed to produce 2023/24 accounts in accordance with its planned timetable'.
findings.matters: Delayed recovery from disclaimer opinions extends the period of financial statement unreliability; falling behind schedule indicates persistent control and capacity issues.
findings.figures: Expected recovery: 2025/26 qualified opinion now delayed to 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council's progress is one year behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01. This is because limited procedures were completed in 2022/23, and then again in 2023/24 when the Council failied to produce 2023/24 accounts in accordance with its planned timetable.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Pension Fund financial statements were not published by the statutory 30 June 2025 deadline, and working papers were of poor quality.
findings.detail: The Pension Fund accounts missed the Accounts and Audit Regulations deadline. Auditors reported that working papers were not of acceptable standard, primarily due to recent changes in the Pension Fund's key finance team. Significant delays occurred in obtaining supporting documentation and evidence.
findings.matters: Pension Fund accounting delays and quality issues reflect management capacity constraints; timeliness failures create regulatory compliance risk.
findings.figures: Deadline missed: 30 June 2025; team changes: recent
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30th June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. The quality of working papers and supporting evidence provided was generally not of an acceptable standard. This was primarily due to recent changes within the Pension Fund's key finance team.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: IFRS 16 Leases implementation remains incomplete; management could not assess voluntary controlled schools adoption in time.
findings.detail: Auditors identified a £790k overstatement in peppercorn leases and £604k in PFI remeasurement differences. Management was unable to complete an assessment of whether voluntary controlled schools should be recognized on the balance sheet in IFRS 16, and these items could not be resolved before the backstop date.
findings.matters: Incomplete lease accounting indicates control environment weakness; unresolved assessments mean potential future restatement risk.
findings.figures: £790k peppercorn lease overstatement; £604k PFI remeasurement difference
findings.quote: Management have not been able to complete this assessment in sufficient time before the backstop date. Other misstatements identified related to overstatement of lease liabilities related to peppercorn leases (£790k overstatement) and a remeasurement difference in PFI lease liabilities (604k overstatement).

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Property, Plant & Equipment valuations contain material errors and the Fixed Asset Register was not completed before draft accounts publication.
findings.detail: Auditors identified £3.7m overstatement between valuers' reports and the FAR, £980k misclassification between asset categories, and £130k net understatement. The FAR was not finalized before the 30 June draft publication, and auditors were unable to fully complete work on material assets under construction before the backstop date.
findings.matters: PPE represents a material asset class; unresolved valuation errors and process failures (late FAR completion) indicate weak asset accounting controls.
findings.figures: £3.7m overstatement (valuers vs FAR); £980k misclassification; £130k net understatement
findings.quote: Other misstatements identified related to overstatement of lease liabilities related to peppercorn leases (£790k overstatement) and a remeasurement difference in PFI lease liabilities (604k overstatement). Furthermore, we were not able to fully complete our work on material assets under construction balances in sufficient time before the backstop.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Adult social care and children's services overspend is persistent and unsustained, consuming corporate contingency.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget required a £7m release of corporate contingency to offset overspends in adult social care and children's services. In 2025/26, the Q1 forecast already shows a £3.4m overspend (1.6% of budget), again primarily driven by these service areas, and the council expects to use the entire £4m corporate contingency.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand-led service pressures indicate loss of budget control in the council's largest expenditure areas; the corporate contingency is a one-time buffer and cannot be relied upon.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £7m released from contingency; 2025/26 Q1: £3.4m overspend forecast; contingency available: £4m
findings.quote: A revised budget was approved at Full Council in February 2025 and included a release of £7m of the corporate contingency to offset the pressures in adult social care and children's services.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: General Reserves are maintained at only £10.6m, providing minimal headroom above the £8m minimum level.
findings.detail: The council's reserves position shows only £2.6m of headroom above the Section 151 officer's minimum of £8m. The auditor describes this as 'very modest level of headroom'. The council has drawn £1.2m in 2024/25 and projects further drawdowns of £700k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Thin reserve coverage limits the council's ability to absorb financial shocks or delayed savings delivery; any adverse variance in the MTFS could force service cuts.
findings.figures: General Reserves £10.6m; minimum level £8m; headroom £2.6m
findings.quote: General Reserves are maintained over the latest MTFS period at not lower than £10.6m, providing a very modest level of headroom to be able to respond to the risks associated with the future cost and funding uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Annual savings requirements are escalating sharply: £2.5m in 2026/27, rising to £6.5m in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The updated MTFS shows savings needs increasing from £2m per annum to £6.5m per annum by 2028/29. The council has a track record of meeting savings targets, but the scale and acceleration of requirements creates delivery risk, particularly given current governance issues.
findings.matters: Escalating, unmet savings requirements are a leading indicator of financial distress; failure to deliver would require further reserve drawdowns or service cuts.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £2.5m; 2028/29: £6.5m (another £2m per annum on prior years)
findings.quote: The MTFS update for 2025/26 to 2028/29 showed an increase in the annual savings requirement to £2.5m in 2026/27, and increasing further to £6.5m in 2028/29, i.e. another £2m per annum.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: The council applied for Exceptional Financial Support of £12.9m for 2026/27 due to escalating cost pressures.
findings.detail: The EFS application indicates the council cannot balance its budget without exceptional government support. This follows a £1.2m drawdown from reserves in 2024/25 and reflects ongoing pressures in adult social care and children's services that are not being contained within budget.
findings.matters: EFS applications signal financial distress and dependency on government support; lenders view this as increased credit risk.
findings.figures: £12.9m EFS applied for 2026/27 (support agreed-in-principle)
findings.quote: For 2026/27 we noted that due to increasing costs pressures the Council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £12.9m (support agreed-in-principle).

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Auditors identified a significant weakness in governance arrangements, including inappropriate member behaviour, breaches of codes of conduct, and dysfunction affecting decision-making.
findings.detail: An independent governance review commissioned by the council found inappropriate behaviour at meetings, poor officer/member interface, lack of support to members, and policies not being used to address breaches. MHCLG expressed concerns about a 17 September 2025 meeting and the potential for a best value notice or inspection. The review concluded this has been 'symptomatic of dysfunction'.
findings.matters: Governance dysfunction directly affects financial decision-making quality, increases reputational risk, and creates potential for regulatory intervention and best value inspection.
findings.figures: Meeting of concern: 17 September 2025; review date: November 2025
findings.quote: Time and resources are being taken up by these issues, including unquantifiable costs of time, reputational damage, and delays in decision making that could have financial implications. The independent report concluded it has been symptomatic of dysfunction.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Annual Report 2025
findings.headline: Auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, with no reasonable assurance over material balances and movements.
findings.detail: Following a disclaimer on 2023/24, auditors lack assurance over opening balances from the prior year and all 2024/25 in-year movements and comparatives. The shortfall stems from incomplete evidence gathering and the statutory backstop date. This is the second consecutive year of disclaimer opinion.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on the audited accounts for credit assessment; the council's financial position is materially uncertain.
findings.figures: 2024/25 and 2023/24 both issued disclaimer opinions; progress is one year behind LARRIG 01 schedule.
findings.quote: we are unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement of the financial statements. We therefore issued a disclaimer 2024/25 audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: 9. Appendix 1 - Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: Council has provided £5m credit facility commitment to Sovereign Network Homes
findings.detail: In June 2024, Isle of Wight Council joined other local authorities in establishing a credit facility for Sovereign Network Homes, committing £5m available for drawing over 3 years with optional 2-year extension. The council receives a non-utilization fee and interest at 2.5% above Bank of England base rate if drawn. As of end-December 2025, no funds have been drawn.
findings.matters: This creates contingent borrowing exposure: if SNH draws on the facility, the council's debt increases by up to £5m. It also represents credit risk exposure to an external organization.
findings.figures: £5m committed facility, currently undrawn
findings.quote: the council has agreed to provide a £5m credit facility for Sovereign Network Homes. This facility is for a period of 3 years with the option of an extension for a further two years.

findings.paper_title: 9. Appendix 1 - Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: Council must exit £37.1m commercial property investments before taking additional borrowing
findings.detail: The council holds £37.1m in commercial investments for financial return, purchased before the 2021 CIPFA Code restricted such borrowing. The treasury strategy requires review of exit options for these assets before the council can undertake further additional borrowing, effectively constraining access to new capital funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital funding plans are constrained by forced asset sales or borrowing restrictions. This dependency indicates compliance pressure and potential impact on capital spend.
findings.figures: £37.1m in commercial investments held for financial return
findings.quote: Before undertaking further additional borrowing the council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: 9. Appendix 1 - Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: Council cash liquidity falls £7.8m short of its self-imposed three-month buffer target
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, cash available within 3 months was £24.0m against the council's target of £31.8m. This failure to meet the council's own voluntary liquidity measure suggests reduced cash flexibility to handle unexpected payments or expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council maintains adequate liquid reserves to meet obligations during market stress. Falling 25% short of self-imposed buffers signals cash management tightness.
findings.figures: Actual cash available £24.0m, target £31.8m, shortfall £7.8m
findings.quote: Total cash available within 3 months 24.0 31.8 No

findings.paper_title: 9. Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: Investment interest rates declining from 4.58% to 3.99% as economic environment softens
findings.detail: The average rate earned on the council's investment portfolio has fallen significantly over nine months, reflecting an environment of falling interest rates, despite investment holdings increasing by £4m.
findings.matters: Declining investment yields will reduce treasury gains available to offset budget pressures going forward; the council's ability to use treasury performance to mitigate deficits is diminishing.
findings.figures: Investment rate declined from 4.58% to 3.99%; investment holdings increased £4m
findings.quote: Over the period of this report the average interest rates on investments, have decreased from an average of 4.58% to 3.99%.

findings.paper_title: 9. Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: Council holds loans to two other local authorities as part of treasury strategy
findings.detail: The council is holding loans advanced to two other councils as part of its investment portfolio. The council monitors their financial position and avoids lending to any authority that has issued a S114 notice.
findings.matters: Represents counterparty concentration risk; loss of either borrower would mean loss of both principal and income. The mention of S114 notice monitoring suggests awareness of council financial stress in the sector.
findings.figures: Loans to 2 local authorities (specific amounts not disclosed)
findings.quote: In addition to investing in money market funds the council has loans advanced to two other local authorities. Close attention is taken to the financial situation of other local authorities, and no loans have been made to any authority that has issued a S114 notice.

findings.paper_title: 9. Treasury Management Report Q3 25-26
findings.headline: £2.9 million treasury gain being used to offset wider council in-year budget pressures
findings.detail: Lower than budgeted borrowing costs and investment income combined to save £2.9m, which the council is deploying to help mitigate budget pressures across the wider authority. This reveals the council is managing in-year financial stress.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council is facing in-year budget pressures severe enough to require treasury gains as an offset, signalling potential structural budget stress.
findings.figures: £2.9 million saving; investment holdings increased £4m during nine-month period; borrowing costs lower than budget
findings.quote: The combination of reduced borrowing costs and increased investment income has resulted in a net forecast saving of £2.9 million contributing to mitigating wider council in-year budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Newport Harbour regeneration previously investigated for housing but found not viable due to prohibitive infrastructure costs
findings.detail: The council previously investigated regeneration of Newport Harbour including substantial housing development but concluded it is not viable. Development would require extensive rebuilding of the harbour wall, but the cost is described as prohibitive. This leaves a significant strategic asset non-productive.
findings.matters: A major harbour-front asset remains unproductive due to identified but unresolved infrastructure cost barriers that prevent development or disposal
findings.figures: cost of harbour wall rebuilding described as prohibitive
findings.quote: To enable such development, extensive rebuilding of the harbour wall is required the cost of which is prohibitive

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Multiple former municipal tips and contaminated sites carry environmental liabilities with uncertain remediation costs
findings.detail: The council holds several former municipal tips and contaminated sites including Stag Lane tip and East Yar Road tip. One site has 'little or no record of what is within the land.' Disposal of these sites is noted as subject to necessary site remediation, creating contingent costs.
findings.matters: Environmental liabilities on council-owned land create contingent costs and delay capital receipts until remediation is completed and disclosed
findings.figures: Multiple sites across Isle of Wight
findings.quote: Former municipal tip (little or no record of what is within the land)

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Key disposals including Thompson House and Weston Academy are conditional on third-party decisions
findings.detail: Thompson House contracts are exchanged but conditional on Southern Water adopting a private drain; Weston Academy is exchanged conditional on planning consent. These major disposals have realization dependent on third parties and could fail to complete if conditions are not met.
findings.matters: Capital receipt timing and certainty is dependent on third-party actions beyond council control, creating risk to capital forecasting
findings.figures: 14 units at Thompson House; 16 units at Weston Academy
findings.quote: Contracts exchanged conditional upon Southern Water confirming the adoption of the existing private drain.

findings.headline: Shanklin Elmdon housing site experienced withdrawn offers after being marketed to developers
findings.detail: The site had received planning consent for 10 houses and was marketed to developers as part of the disposal pipeline. Developer offers were subsequently withdrawn and the council now needs to reconsider the approach. This signals market difficulty in disposing of planned housing sites.
findings.matters: Market rejection of housing development sites indicates pricing, demand, or viability challenges that could delay capital receipts or require write-down of value expectations
findings.figures: 10 houses (planning consent received)
findings.quote: The site has been marketed and a decision made to appoint a developer. However offers have been withdrawn and now need to reconsider the best way forward for this site.
